---
title: Diseases
jupyter: python3
---

Diseases are the core of most Starsim models: they define the states a person can be in (e.g. susceptible, infected, recovered), how people move between those states, and, for communicable diseases, how infection spreads through the population and its [networks](modules_networks.qmd). This page covers the two ways to write a disease (declared from states and transitions, or written as code), the per-agent quantities every infection shares (including `rel_sus` and `rel_trans`), and the patterns for customizing or building your own disease.

For a learning-oriented introduction, see [Tutorial 4 - Diseases](../tutorials/t4_diseases.qmd).

## Two ways to write a disease

| | Declared | Written as code |
|---|---|---|
| Base class | `ss.Disease` | `ss.Infection` (or `ss.NCD`) |
| What you write | states and the transitions between them | per-agent arrays (`define_states()`) and the methods that update them (`set_prognoses()`, `step_state()`) |
| Solvers | any: `'ode'`, `'binomial'`, `'gillespie'`, `'abm'` (`'auto'` picks one) | agents |
| Inspection | `describe()`, `equations()`, `diagram()`, `R0()` | `describe()` in brief |
| Library examples | `ss.SIR`, `ss.SIS`, `ss.SEIR` | `ssl.HIV`, `ssl.Ebola`, `ssl.Cholera`, and Starsim 3's SIR, SEIR, and SIS as `ssl.AgentSIR`, `ssl.AgentSEIR`, `ssl.AgentSIS` |

Both are first-class, and both kinds can be in the same sim. Declare a disease when it can be said as states and transitions; write it as code when it needs per-agent quantities that change continuously (a CD4 count, a level of immunity that wanes, a viral load). Whether a disease is declared is decided by its class: `ss.Disease` is only for declared diseases, and a disease written as code subclasses `ss.Infection`.

## Declared diseases

### States and transitions, in three spellings

A declared disease is a set of states and the transitions between them. There is one transition class, `ss.Transition`, and three ways to write one, which all build the same model:

```{python}
import starsim as ss
ss.options(jupyter=True)

# 1. Arrow strings: the states are read from the strings
sir1 = ss.Disease(
    infection = ss.transmission('S -> I', beta=0.3),
    recovery  = ss.progression('I -> R', dur=ss.days(10)),
    init_prev = 0.01,
    name = 'sir',
)

# 2. Operators: the states are declared first, then used like the equations
S, I, R = ss.states(3)
infection = S >> I @ 0.3 * I # "S goes to I at rate 0.3 times I"
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(10) # A duration after @ is a mean time in the state
sir2 = ss.Disease(infection, recovery, init_prev=0.01, name='sir')

# 3. Fully explicit
sir3 = ss.Disease(
    ss.Transition(S, I, rate=0.3 * I, name='infection'),
    ss.Transition(I, R, dur=ss.days(10), name='recovery'),
    init_prev = 0.01,
    name = 'sir',
)

for sir in [sir1, sir2, sir3]:
    sim = ss.Sim(sir, stop=100, verbose=0).run()
    print(f'Peak infected: {sim.results.sir.n_I.max():,.0f}')
```

The first spelling is the short form for SIR-shaped models, the second is the one to use for everything else, and the third is for building models programmatically. States, transitions, and the disease take their names from the variables they are assigned to (or from the keyword they are passed under); give `name=` when a disease is built inline.

A bare state inside a rate (`0.3 * I`) means contact with people in that state: with no network that is `I.n / N`, the share of the population who are infectious, so `S >> I @ beta * I` is the textbook `beta * S * I / N`. With a network or a contact matrix, the same expression is worked out from whom each person actually meets, and `beta` is per contact. `I.n` is the number of people in `I`, used exactly as written. In the arrow-string form the word `transmission` stands for "times the source": `ss.transmission('S -> I', beta=b)` is `S >> I @ b * I`.

Every declared disease gets a result for each state (`n_S`, `n_I`, `n_R`) and a flow for each transition, named after it (`infection`, `recovery`), with its running total as `.cum`.

### Looking at the model

Because the model is made of objects, its description, equations, and transition table are derived from it:

```{python}
sir = sir1
sir.equations()
sir.transitions
```

`sim.describe()` shows the whole sim as Starsim has read it, with every default it filled in marked as a guess:

```{python}
ss.Sim(sir, stop=100).describe()
```

### The library's SIR, SIS, and SEIR

`ss.SIR`, `ss.SIS`, and `ss.SEIR` are declared diseases with Starsim's keywords (`beta`, `init_prev`, `dur_inf`, `p_death`, and `dur_exp` for SEIR), so they run with any solver. As well as the counts and flows of their states and transitions, they keep Starsim's standard results, `new_infections`, `cum_infections`, and `prevalence`:

```{python}
sir = ss.SIR(beta=0.1, dur_inf=ss.years(6), init_prev=0.01)
sim = ss.Sim(sir, networks='random', n_agents=5_000, start='2000', stop='2040', verbose=0)
sim.run()
print(sim.results.sir.keys())
sim.results.sir.plot()
```

Their states are `S`, `I`, `R` (and `E` for SEIR), with the Starsim 3 names `susceptible`, `infected`, and `recovered` as aliases. Starsim 3's versions of these diseases, written as code, are `ssl.AgentSIR`, `ssl.AgentSIS`, and `ssl.AgentSEIR` (below).

### Dwell times

A duration means an exponentially distributed time in the state with that mean, as in an ODE; `describe()` marks this as a guess. Any distribution of durations can be given instead:

```{python}
S, I, R = ss.states(3)
recoveries = dict(
    exponential = I >> R @ ss.days(10),
    erlang      = I >> R @ ss.erlang(k=3, mean=ss.days(10)),
    lognormal   = I >> R @ ss.lognorm_ex(mean=10, std=3, unit='days'),
)
for label, recovery in recoveries.items():
    sir = ss.Disease(infection=S >> I @ 0.3 * I, recovery=recovery, init_prev=0.01, name='sir')
    sim = ss.Sim(sir, stop=ss.days(100), verbose=0).run()
    print(f'{label:12s} peak infected: {sim.results.sir.n_I.max():,.0f}')
```

As agents, each person draws their own time in the state. In a compartmental run, an Erlang distribution is realized exactly as stages, and any other distribution is approximated by Erlang stages matched to its mean and variance, with a note. `stages=k` on a transition (`ss.progression('I -> R', dur=ss.days(10), stages=3)`) uses `k` stages under every solver, agents included.

### Branching

Transitions out of one state that carry `p=` split on entry, and each branch can have its own time in the state. Transitions out of one state that carry only rates compete as hazards. In the operator form, a weight on the destination is the branch probability:

```{python}
S, I, H, R = ss.states(4)
infection = S >> I @ ss.perday(0.3) * I
severe    = I >> 0.1 * H @ ss.days(5)  # 10% go to hospital after 5 days on average
mild      = I >> 0.9 * R @ ss.days(10) # the rest recover after 10
discharge = H >> R @ ss.days(14)
covid = ss.Disease(infection, severe, mild, discharge, init_prev=0.001)

sim = ss.Sim(covid, stop=ss.days(200), verbose=0).run()
res = sim.results.covid
print(f'Hospitalized: {res.severe.sum():,.0f}; recovered without hospital: {res.mild.sum():,.0f}; peak in hospital: {res.n_H.max():,.0f}')
```

Death from infection is a branch to `ss.null`, which stands for outside the model: `ss.Transition(I, R, dur=dur, p=0.99)` and `ss.Transition(I, ss.null, dur=dur, p=0.01)`. This is how `ss.SIR` implements `p_death`.

### Births and deaths in a disease

Births and deaths of everyone are declared for the population, in `ss.Sim(demographics=[...])`, so the same people are born into and die from every disease ([Demographics](modules_demographics.qmd)). With one disease, they can also be declared in the disease itself, as an inflow and an outflow. `ss.birth(rate=r)` is a crude birth rate (per person per unit time) into a state, and `ss.death(rate=r)` with no arrow applies to every state that is people:

```{python}
S, I, R = ss.states(3)
sirs = ss.Disease(
    infection = S >> I @ ss.peryear(20) * I,
    recovery  = I >> R @ ss.weeks(2),
    waning    = R >> S @ ss.years(5),
    births    = ss.birth('-> S', rate=ss.peryear(0.03)),
    deaths    = ss.death(rate=ss.peryear(0.02)),
    init_prev = 0.001,
)
sim = ss.Sim(sirs, start='2000', stop='2050', verbose=0).run()
sim.results.sirs.plot()
```

This works under every solver. For realistic demographics (fertility and mortality by age and year, pregnancy), use the demographics modules instead; see [Demographics](modules_demographics.qmd).

### States that are not people

Some of what a disease model tracks is not people: bacteria in water, a mosquito population. These are ordinary states in the same disease. A state that no transition connects to the disease's first state is a count, not people: it is never represented as agents, is not part of the population size, and is used in rates as a count (`W.n`). Here is Codeço's cholera model, with bacteria shed into the water by infectious people:

```{python}
beta = 0.5 # Infection hazard per day at saturating exposure
K    = 1e5 # Concentration (cells/mL) giving half the maximum hazard
xi   = 10  # Cells/mL shed per infectious person per day

S, I, R, W = ss.states(4) # W is bacteria in the water
cholera = ss.Disease(
    infection = S >> I @ beta * W.n / (W.n + K),
    recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(5),
    shedding  = ss.null >> W @ xi * I.n,    # An inflow: a total per day
    decay     = W >> ss.null @ ss.days(30), # Mean lifetime in the water
    init      = dict(I=0.001),
)
sim = ss.Sim(cholera, total_pop=100_000, unit='day', stop=365)
sim.describe()
```

### The class form

A disease can also be written as a class, with its states, parameters, and transitions in the class body. This is the form for a disease that goes into a library, or that needs a method as well as transitions (override `step()` and call `super().step()` to run the declared transitions):

```{python}
class SEIR(ss.Disease):
    S, E, I, R = ss.states(4)
    beta     = ss.par(ss.perday(0.3), bounds=[0.1, 1]) # Bounds make it fittable with sim.calibrate()
    exposure = S >> E @ beta * I
    onset    = E >> I @ ss.days(5)
    recovery = I >> R @ ss.days(10)

seir = SEIR(init_prev=0.01) # Named "seir", after the class
sim = ss.Sim(seir, stop=ss.days(200), verbose=0).run()
sim.results.seir.plot()
```

## Susceptibility and transmissibility

Every infection, declared or written as code, has two per-agent arrays that set each person's risk:

| Name | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| `rel_sus` | Per-agent **relative susceptibility** (default `1.0`) |
| `rel_trans` | Per-agent **relative transmissibility** (default `1.0`) |

On a network, the hazard of infection along an edge from an infectious source to a susceptible target is, in essence, $\beta \times \texttt{rel\_trans}_{\text{source}} \times \texttt{rel\_sus}_{\text{target}}$, and the probability of infection over a step follows from it. Only infectious people contribute their `rel_trans`, and only susceptible people their `rel_sus`; both default to 1, so by default transmission is governed by `beta` and the network.

These two arrays are the standard "knobs" that the rest of the framework turns to represent heterogeneity in risk. For example:

- A [vaccine](modules_products.qmd) reduces `rel_sus` for the people who hold it.
- A treatment might reduce `rel_trans` for the people on it.
- A [modifier](modules_connectors.qmd) between two diseases might increase `rel_sus` to one disease for people infected with another, with `ss.modify(sis.rel_sus, multiply=3, where=hiv.infected)`.
- A declared state can carry its own multipliers, e.g. `V = ss.State(rel_sus=0.2)` for a partially protected state.

Because they're ordinary per-agent arrays, you can also set them directly. Here we fully protect everyone under 20 by setting their `rel_sus` to 0, and see that they avoid infection (aside from the handful seeded as infected at the start via `init_prev`):

```{python}
sir = ss.SIR(init_prev=0.01)
sim = ss.Sim(n_agents=2000, diseases=sir, networks='random', copy_inputs=False, verbose=0)
sim.init()

# Fully protect under-20s: rel_sus = 0 means they cannot acquire infection
young = (sim.people.age < 20).uids
older = (sim.people.age >= 20).uids
sir.rel_sus[young] = 0.0

sim.run()
ever_infected = sir.ti_I.notnan # The time each agent entered I
print(f'Protected (under 20): {ever_infected[young].sum()} of {len(young)} ever infected')
print(f'Unprotected (20+):    {ever_infected[older].sum()} of {len(older)} ever infected')
```

Assigning sets the *base* value; modifiers made with `ss.modify` apply on top of it without overwriting it (see [Connectors](modules_connectors.qmd)).

:::{.callout-note}
`beta` can be given per network and per direction. For sexually transmitted infections, for example, `beta={'mf': [0.25, 0.15]}` sets different male→female and female→male values on the `mf` network. See the [Networks](modules_networks.qmd) page for more.
:::

:::{.callout-warning}
In Starsim 4, `beta` is a rate per unit time (per contact, when there are networks), whether it is a bare number or typed (`ss.peryear(0.1)`), including the values in a dict given per network. In Starsim 3 a dict of bare numbers was a probability per step, so a dict copied from a Starsim 3 model with steps shorter than its unit is too low by a factor of about `1/dt`; give its values their Starsim 3 meaning explicitly, e.g. `beta={'random': ss.prob(0.05, 'month')}`. See the [migration guide](../migration/v3_v4.md).
:::

## Diseases written as code

A disease written as code subclasses `ss.Disease` and declares nothing (it defines its states with `define_states()` and what happens each step in `step_state()` and `step()`, as Starsim 3's `ss.Disease`), or, if it is transmitted between agents, `ss.Infection`, which provides network transmission (with per-network, per-direction `beta`), `rel_sus` and `rel_trans`, and the infection log. Starsim 3's SIR, SEIR, and SIS are available in this form as `ssl.AgentSIR`, `ssl.AgentSEIR`, and `ssl.AgentSIS` (`import starsim.library as ssl`), and are the usual starting point; a Starsim 3 subclass of `ss.SIR` that overrides its methods can subclass `ssl.AgentSIR` instead, unchanged.

**Important:** Do **not** write your own `infect()` method unless you have very specific requirements. The built-in method correctly handles looping over the networks, applying network- and disease-specific transmission, agent susceptibility and transmissibility, and mixing pools.

### Key implementation methods

| Method | Purpose | When to override |
|--------|---------|------------------|
| `define_states()` | Initialize additional disease states | When adding states not supplied by the base class |
| `set_prognoses()` | Set outcomes for newly infected people | For fully custom acquisition logic; call `super()` |
| `step_state()` | Update states each timestep | When adding new state transitions |
| `step_die()` | Handle deaths | When disease has custom states |
| `infect()` | Handle transmission | **Rarely** - use built-in version |

### Core states and parameters

Every `ss.Infection` shares a common set of per-agent states and parameters:

| Name | Type | Meaning |
|------|------|---------|
| `susceptible` | `BoolState` | Whether an agent can be infected (default `True`) |
| `infected` | `BoolState` | Whether an agent currently has the infection |
| `infectious` | alias | Agents that can currently transmit (by default, an alias of `infected`) |
| `rel_sus` | `FloatArr` | Per-agent relative susceptibility (default `1.0`) |
| `rel_trans` | `FloatArr` | Per-agent relative transmissibility (default `1.0`) |
| `ti_infected` | `FloatArr` | Time point at which each agent acquired the infection: the end of the step it happened in (`self.ti_entry`), as for a declared disease |
| `beta` | parameter | Transmission rate per contact (per network) |
| `init_prev` | parameter | Initial fraction of the population infected |

:::{.callout-note}
In a module written as code, `self.ti` inside `step_state()` and `set_prognoses()` is the time point at the *start* of the step, as in Starsim 3. Results are recorded at the end of the step: in `update_results()`, `self.ti` is the step's end, so an event dated during the step has a time of `self.ti - 1`. Infections are the exception: set `ti_infected` (and schedule what follows) from `self.ti_entry`, the end of the step, since the infection has happened by then; a declared disease dates `ti_I` the same way, so in `update_results()` this step's infections are `ti_infected == self.ti`. (Starsim 3 dated them at the start, so an infection with a duration of one step was never infectious.) See [Analyzers](modules_analyzers.qmd).
:::

### Infected vs. infectious

Transmission comes from `infectious` agents. For an SIR model "infected" and "infectious" are the same thing, so `ss.Infection` declares `infectious` as an **alias** of `infected`:

```python
self.define_states(
    ss.BoolState('susceptible', default=True, label='Susceptible'),
    ss.BoolState('infected', label='Infected'),
    ...
    infectious = 'infected', # Everyone infected is infectious, unless a subclass says otherwise
)
```

An alias is only consulted when the attribute isn't otherwise defined, so it's a default that a subclass can replace, either with a state of its own or with another alias. That's what `ssl.AgentSEIR` does: for a disease with a latent period the two names come apart, since **E and I are both infected, but only I is infectious**. So `ssl.AgentSEIR` makes `exposed` and `infectious` the literal E and I compartments, and derives `infected` from them:

```python
self.define_states(
    ss.BoolState('exposed', label='Exposed'),
    ss.BoolState('infectious', label='Infectious'),
    ...
    reset = ['infected', 'infectious', 'ti_infected'],
    infected = lambda self: self.exposed | self.infectious, # Derived: E and I are both infected
)
```

A callable alias behaves like a property: it takes the module as its only argument and is recomputed on each access, so it can be read but not written to. Unlike a string alias, it generates an automatic result, so `n_infected` still exists and counts E plus I. See [Aliases](modules_adding.qmd#aliases) for more. (The declared `ss.SEIR` follows the same convention: its `infected` is `E | I`, and only `I` is a source of infection.)

Incidence is a separate concept from any compartment. `ss.Infection.set_prognoses()` records each infection as it happens, so `new_infections` doesn't depend on what a model does with the `ti_` states or how many stages it has. Seed infections from `init_prev` are prevalent cases, and are excluded from incidence.

The result is that each name means one thing:

- `n_exposed` is the E compartment and `n_infectious` is the I compartment, while `n_infected` and `prevalence` cover both: an agent in the latent period has the infection, and counts towards prevalence.
- `ti_exposed` is the time of acquisition and `ti_infectious` is the time of becoming infectious. In general, `ti_<state>` is the time the agent entered `<state>`.
- `ssl.AgentSEIR` deliberately does **not** define `ti_infected`, since it is too easily confused with `ti_infectious`; use `ti_exposed` for the time of acquisition.
- `new_infections` counts infection events (S→E for SEIR, S→I for SIR).

If you wanted presymptomatic transmission instead, so that exposed agents transmit too, you would override the states that drive transmission rather than the ones that define infection, for example by giving exposed agents a nonzero `rel_trans`.

### Pattern 1: Extending an existing disease

When you need to modify a disease written as code, inherit from it and override specific methods:

```{python}
import starsim.library as ssl

class MyCustomSIR(ssl.AgentSIR):
    def __init__(self, **kwargs):
        super().__init__()
        # Add custom parameters
        self.define_pars(my_param=0.5)
        self.update_pars(**kwargs)

    def set_prognoses(self, uids, sources=None):
        # Custom progression logic
        super().set_prognoses(uids, sources)
        # Additional custom logic here
```

### Pattern 2: Extending an SEIR model

For a disease with a latent period, start from `ssl.AgentSEIR`. A simple model needs only new parameter defaults:

```{python}
class MySEIR(ssl.AgentSEIR):
    def __init__(self, **kwargs):
        super().__init__()
        self.define_pars(
            dur_exp = ss.lognorm_ex(ss.years(0.5)),
            dur_inf = ss.lognorm_ex(ss.years(1.0)),
        )
        self.update_pars(**kwargs)

sim = ss.Sim(diseases=MySEIR(init_prev=0.05), networks='random', start='2000', stop='2020', verbose=0)
sim.run()
sim.diseases.myseir.plot()
```

(The same model declared is `ss.SEIR(dur_exp=ss.lognorm_ex(ss.years(0.5)), dur_inf=ss.lognorm_ex(ss.years(1.0)), init_prev=0.05)`, which also runs as an ODE.)

For a richer natural history, `ssl.AgentSIR.set_prognoses()` splits into two methods you can override separately:

| Method | Purpose |
|--------|---------|
| `set_infection(uids)` | Make agents infectious. `ssl.AgentSEIR` overrides this to put them in `exposed` first, and set `ti_infectious` to the end of the latent period. |
| `set_progression(uids)` | Schedule what happens next: recovery, death, and any other stages. Schedule these relative to the onset of infectiousness (`ti_infected` in `ssl.AgentSIR`, `ti_infectious` in `ssl.AgentSEIR`), so that a latent period delays them rather than eating into them. |

`ssl.Ebola` and `ssl.Cholera` both override `set_progression()` for their extra states (severe/buried and symptomatic respectively), and inherit everything else from `ssl.AgentSEIR`.

If your model adds a compartment, list it in `plot_states` so that `disease.plot()` shows it. This is a class attribute holding the names of the results to plot, so it can be set in one line at the top of the class body: `ssl.AgentSEIR` sets `plot_states = ['n_susceptible', 'n_exposed', 'n_infectious', 'n_recovered']`. Assign a new list rather than modifying the inherited one, since a class attribute is shared by every instance of the class.
